reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents with progressive impairment of higher visual and spatial processing, with early memory and insight relatively preserved
Patients struggle with reading, judging distances, locating objects and dressing, despite normal basic acuity and eyes, reflecting cortical rather than ocular visual failure
Features may include components of Balint syndrome (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia) and Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation)
Onset is often at a relatively young age, and patients are frequently referred first to ophthalmology because the problem seems visual
Alzheimer disease is the most common underlying pathology, though corticobasal degeneration, Lewy body disease and prion disease can also produce the syndrome
Imaging shows atrophy and hypometabolism concentrated in the parieto-occipital and posterior temporal cortex
Amyloid imaging and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers help confirm underlying Alzheimer pathology
reference.pathophysiology: Posterior cortical atrophy is a clinical-radiological syndrome caused by neurodegeneration concentrated in the posterior cortical regions responsible for higher-order visual and spatial processing, including the occipital, parietal and posterior temporal lobes. The commonest underlying pathology is Alzheimer disease, in which amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles accumulate predominantly in these posterior networks rather than the medial temporal memory regions, producing a visual-predominant rather than amnestic phenotype. Progressive damage to the dorsal and ventral visual pathways disrupts the integration of visual information, spatial localisation and object recognition, while primary visual acuity and the eyes themselves remain intact.
additionalDifferentials: Primary ophthalmological or optic pathway disease
Occipital stroke or structural posterior lesion
Delirium or a primary psychiatric disorder
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to demonstrate parieto-occipital and posterior temporal atrophy
FDG-PET to show posterior cortical hypometabolism
Amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and tau markers to confirm Alzheimer pathology
Formal ophthalmological and visual acuity assessment to exclude primary eye disease
Detailed neuropsychological testing of visuospatial and higher visual functions
Assessment for parkinsonian or myoclonic features suggesting alternative pathology
redFlags: Rapid progression or myoclonus raising concern for prion disease
Development of parkinsonism or asymmetrical limb apraxia suggesting corticobasal degeneration
Visual disability causing falls, driving hazards and loss of independence
Marked fluctuations or visual hallucinations pointing to Lewy body disease
reference.prognosis: Posterior cortical atrophy is progressive, with worsening visual and spatial disability and eventual spread to involve broader cognitive domains resembling more generalised dementia; prognosis reflects the underlying pathology, and management is supportive with visual aids, environmental adaptation and caregiver support.
pitfalls: Repeatedly investigating the eyes when the problem is cortical visual processing
Missing the diagnosis because early memory and insight are preserved
Assuming all cases are Alzheimer disease without considering Lewy body, corticobasal or prion pathology
Underestimating the safety impact of cortical visual failure on driving and daily living
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Offer cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine where underlying Alzheimer pathology is confirmed, as for typical Alzheimer dementia
Provide occupational therapy and environmental adaptation (decluttering, high-contrast markings, consistent object placement) to compensate for the visuospatial deficit
Supply low-vision aids and reading and navigation strategies, recognising the failure is cortical rather than ocular
Treat associated depression and anxiety with psychological support and antidepressants as needed
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, ophthalmology, occupational therapy and cognitive services, with early involvement given the often young onset
Monitor for spread to broader cognitive domains and for emergent parkinsonian or myoclonic features suggesting an alternative underlying pathology
Provide carer support, driving cessation advice and advance care planning
